questions.question: Which HTTP method is idempotent but NOT safe (i.e. it changes server state, but repeating it has the same effect as doing it once)?

choices.text: GET
PUT
POST
PATCH

questions.explanation: PUT replaces a resource with a given representation — calling it once or N times leaves the resource in the same end state, so it's idempotent, but it does change server state, so it isn't safe. GET is both safe and idempotent (read-only). POST and PATCH are neither safe nor idempotent by default: POST /orders twice creates two orders, and a PATCH expressed as a delta (e.g. "increment counter") is not idempotent either.

questions.question: How long does Stripe retain the result of an idempotency key before it can be reused for a brand-new operation?

choices.text: 5 minutes
1 hour
24 hours
Forever — keys are never expired

questions.explanation: Stripe retains idempotency keys for at least 24 hours, which comfortably covers realistic client retry/backoff windows (including a client retrying after being offline overnight) without keeping unbounded state forever. After that window, reusing the same key is treated as a new operation, not a replay.

questions.question: What does the `Cache-Control: no-cache` directive actually mean?

choices.text: The response must never be stored by any HTTP cache at any layer
The response is cached but must be revalidated before each reuse
The response can be cached, but only for a maximum of one second
It behaves exactly the same as the no-store directive

questions.explanation: Despite the name, `no-cache` does NOT mean "don't cache." Per RFC 9111, it means the response may be stored, but must not be used to satisfy a later request without first being revalidated with the origin server — the revalidation is what makes it feel like "no caching" in practice even though storage is allowed. `no-store` (option d) is the directive that actually forbids storage entirely — a very common point of confusion. There's no built-in 1-second cap (option c), and outright banning storage (option a) is what `no-store` does, not `no-cache`.

questions.question: Which of the following requests will NOT trigger a CORS preflight (i.e. qualifies as a "simple request")?

choices.text: A POST with Content-Type: application/json
A GET with a custom X-Api-Key header
A POST with Content-Type: text/plain and no custom headers
A PUT request with Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

questions.explanation: A "simple request" is limited to GET/HEAD/POST, no custom headers, and a Content-Type of only application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, or text/plain. A POST with text/plain and no custom headers qualifies. application/json is NOT in that allowed list (so option a triggers a preflight), any custom header triggers a preflight (option b), and PUT is not one of the three allowed simple methods (option d).

questions.question: Why was the OAuth 2.0 implicit grant deprecated in favor of authorization code + PKCE for public clients like SPAs?

choices.text: It doesn't support issuing refresh tokens to the client
It exposes the access token via the redirect URI fragment
It requires a confidential client secret that public clients can't store
It performs noticeably slower than the authorization code flow

questions.explanation: RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP) formally deprecates the implicit grant because it returns the token directly in the URI fragment with no back-channel exchange step, exposing it to browser history, referrer leakage, and malicious browser extensions. PKCE fixes this by keeping the token exchange server-side and requiring a cryptographic verifier the original requester alone holds. Option c describes a real constraint of public clients like SPAs (they can't hold a client secret at all), but that's a separate reason authorization code + PKCE — not client credentials — is used; it's not why implicit specifically was deprecated. Option a is false (implicit simply never issued refresh tokens, which isn't the security rationale), and option d is not the stated concern in the BCP.

questions.question: In the token bucket rate-limiting algorithm, what does the bucket's capacity (B) control?

choices.text: The steady long-term average rate of allowed requests
The maximum burst size allowed above the steady rate
The HTTP status code returned once the bucket is empty
How frequently the bucket receives new tokens

questions.explanation: The refill rate (R tokens/second, option a) controls the steady long-term average rate; the bucket capacity (B) controls how large a burst can be spent at once before the client has to wait for refills. This is exactly why token bucket is preferred over a naive fixed-window counter, which allows an unintended 2x burst right at a window boundary. Option c (status code) and option d (refill frequency, which is what the rate R actually governs) are both unrelated to what capacity specifically controls.

questions.question: Why does cursor-based (keyset) pagination stay fast at deep pages while offset-based pagination gets slower the deeper you page?

choices.text: Cursor pagination automatically caches results in Redis
Offset scans and discards all skipped rows; cursor jumps via an index
Cursor pagination works without needing any index at all
Offset pagination performance doesn't depend on page depth

questions.explanation: `OFFSET N` still requires the database to scan and discard the first N rows before returning results, so deep pages get progressively slower — the opposite of option d. Cursor/keyset pagination instead issues an indexed `WHERE id > :cursor ORDER BY id LIMIT N` query, which stays roughly constant-time regardless of how deep you page, because it jumps directly to the right place in the index rather than scanning from the start — it relies on that index (contradicting option c), not on an external cache (option a).

questions.question: HTTP/2 solves HTTP/1.1's head-of-line blocking at the application layer via multiplexed streams. What limitation remains even with HTTP/2?

choices.text: HTTP/2 only allows a single request per connection at a time
A lost TCP segment still stalls every stream on that connection
HTTP/2 opens a brand-new connection for every stream it multiplexes
There is no remaining limitation left for HTTP/2 to solve

questions.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes independent streams over a single TCP connection, fixing HOL blocking at the HTTP layer — the opposite of options a and c, which both misdescribe how HTTP/2 multiplexing works. But because all those streams still share one TCP connection, and TCP guarantees strictly in-order byte delivery, a single lost/delayed TCP segment stalls delivery for every stream on that connection — TCP-level HOL blocking remains, so option d is wrong too. HTTP/3, built on QUIC/UDP, was designed specifically to give each stream independent loss recovery and eliminate this.

questions.question: What HTTP header is used to communicate the exact date/time an API version will stop working, as part of a deprecation timeline?

choices.text: Deprecation
Sunset
Retry-After
X-API-Version

questions.explanation: RFC 8594 defines the `Sunset` header, which a server includes on responses to signal the exact date/time an endpoint or resource will stop being available — typically paired with a `Link` header pointing to migration docs. After the sunset date passes, the endpoint should return `410 Gone`, not a silent `404`.

questions.question: Which of the following are genuine downsides of naive GraphQL usage compared to REST? (select all that apply)

choices.text: A naive resolver implementation can introduce its own N+1 problem
Standard HTTP-level caching (keyed on distinct cacheable URLs) doesn't work the same way against a single POST endpoint
GraphQL cannot express nested/related data in a single request
Clients can construct deeply nested or wide queries that are expensive to resolve if the server doesn't bound query cost

questions.explanation: GraphQL resolvers can introduce their own per-field N+1 problem without batching (e.g. Dataloader-style patterns), a single POST endpoint breaks typical URL-keyed HTTP caching, and uncapped query complexity/depth is a real DoS risk that requires server-side cost analysis or depth limiting. Option c is false — the ability to express nested/related data in one request is GraphQL's core value proposition (solving REST's over-fetching/under-fetching), not a limitation.
